To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the CSA and CSB protein products of the Cockayne syndrome genes are involved in the repair of oxidative DNA damage, both directly and indirectly, and that their mutations result in an accumulation of oxidative DNA damage in the cells and tissues, which is the most likely cause of the symptoms of Cockayne Syndrome.

the CS proteins, in addition to transcription-coupled repair, are involved in the processing of endogenously generated oxidative DNA damage, and that this involvement is mediated by direct interactions with BER proteins and indirect effects on the expression of DNA repair genes.

CSA and CS proteins are involved in the repair of oxidative damage in both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA and that the observed defects are likely to contribute to the clinical symptoms of the disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the CS proteins in the repair of oxidatively generated lesions and the implications for cell death and mutagenesis in CS patients.
the role of the CSA and CSB gene products in the repair of oxidative DNA damage and their potential involvement in the pathophysiology of CS.

the elucidation of the role of CSA and CS proteins in the repair of oxidatively generated damage in nuclear and mitochondrial DNA and their involvement in the maintenance of mitochondrial function and gene transcription.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CS proteins play an important role in the repair of oxidative DNA damage and that this role is likely to be one of the factors responsible for the clinical phenotype of the disease.
CSA and CS proteins are involved in the BER of oxidized DNA, but the exact molecular mechanism of their involvement remains to be elucidated.
CSA and CS proteins are involved in the repair of oxidatively damaged DNA, but the exact nature of their involvement remains to be determined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CS proteins are involved in the repair and/or processing of oxidatively generated damage, and this is important for the survival of cells.
the CS proteins are important for the repair of endogenous DNA damage, especially in mitochondria, and that the resulting genetic instability may contribute to the clinical symptoms of CS.

the CS proteins are important in the cellular response to oxidative stress, but the molecular mechanisms of their action in the DNA repair pathways are still not well defined and require further investigation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

CS patients are not deficient in the repair of DNA damage, but rather in the processing of unrepaired lesions, which results in the accumulation of DNA damage, the induction of cell cycle arrest, and the induction of mutations.
the CS proteins are involved in the repair of DNA damage induced not only by ultraviolet light but also by endogenous agents.
